opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the word "distillation" has gotten stretched quite a bit, and it's worth separating out a few meanings.

The classic definition, going back to Hinton and colleagues, is pretty narrow: you have a teacher model, you take its full output distribution, the soft probabilities over classes or tokens, and you train a student to match that distribution, usually with a KL divergence. The point is that the teacher's probabilities carry much more information than a single hard label. They tell you which wrong answers are almost right, and that "dark knowledge" is what makes the student learn more efficiently.

In the LLM world today, people often use "distillation" much more loosely. A lot of the time it just means: generate a bunch of outputs from a stronger model and do supervised fine-tuning on those samples. That's really sequence-level distillation, or honestly just training on synthetic data. It works, but you're throwing away most of the signal, because you only see one sampled sequence instead of the teacher's full distribution at every token.

The part I find most interesting, and where a lot of my own work has been, is the distribution mismatch problem. If you only train the student on sequences the teacher generated, then at inference the student generates its own sequences, makes mistakes the teacher never would, and ends up in states it never saw during training. That's the classic exposure bias or compounding error problem from imitation learning. So the idea behind on-policy distillation, which is what we did in work like generalized knowledge distillation, is to let the student generate its own outputs and then have the teacher provide token-level feedback on those. You're getting dense supervision on the student's own distribution. It looks a lot like RL, except instead of a sparse scalar reward at the end, you have a teacher telling you at every token how it would have done things.

You can also choose the divergence. Forward KL makes the student cover all the teacher's modes, which can be bad when the student is much smaller and can't represent everything. Reverse KL is more mode-seeking, so the student commits to what it can do well. That choice matters a lot in practice.

So in current research I'd describe distillation as a spectrum. At one end you have cheap off-policy SFT on teacher samples. At the other end you have on-policy, token-level teacher feedback, which sits very close to reinforcement learning. And I think increasingly the frontier labs think of distillation and RL as part of the same toolkit: RL to discover new capabilities in the biggest model, then distillation, ideally on-policy, to transfer them efficiently into smaller, cheaper models people can actually serve.

r001.rationale: The response describes transferring capabilities into smaller models, but does not state that the student can be the same size as the teacher.

r002.rationale: The response describes matching the teacher’s full output distribution and on-policy token-level teacher feedback, showing distillation beyond fine-tuning on teacher-generated samples.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think distillation has become one of those words that means a lot of different things depending on who you ask, and I actually think that's part of why it's interesting right now.

The classic version, the Hinton, Vinyals, Dean version from 2015, is you have a big teacher model, you have a smaller student, and you train the student to match the teacher's output distribution instead of just the hard labels. The idea being that the soft probabilities carry "dark knowledge," information about which wrong answers are plausible, and that's a richer training signal than one-hot labels. That's still a real thing and people still do it.

But I think the way it's used in frontier LLM work today is broader and, honestly, a bit sloppier. Most of what gets called distillation now is really just training on samples from a stronger model. You prompt the teacher, you collect its generations, and you fine-tune the student on those. That's sequence-level knowledge distillation, going back to Kim and Rush, and it's basically supervised fine-tuning on synthetic data. The teacher's logits never enter the picture. So when a lab says a small model is "distilled" from a big one, nine times out of ten they mean this.

The thing I've spent a lot of time thinking about is that this on-policy versus off-policy distinction matters a lot more than people initially assumed. If you only train the student on teacher samples, you're training it on text the student itself would never produce. The student then makes its own mistakes at inference time and has never seen a correction for those mistakes. That's the same exposure bias problem that shows up everywhere in sequence modeling. So the on-policy framing is: let the student generate, and then have the teacher provide a signal on the student's own trajectories, whether that's a token-level KL to the teacher's distribution or some reward. Once you frame it that way, distillation and RL start to look like the same object. The teacher is just a very informative, dense reward model.

And I think that's actually the useful mental model. Distillation is a knowledge transfer mechanism where you're trading off how dense the signal is against how much you trust the teacher. Hard labels, very sparse. Teacher samples, you get full trajectories but it's off-policy. Teacher logits on student samples, dense and on-policy, but you need teacher access and the distributions need to be comparable. RL from a verifier, on-policy and trustworthy but incredibly sparse. These are all points on the same spectrum.

The other thing I'd say is that distillation in the reasoning era has changed what we think the "knowledge" being transferred is. With the R1-style work, what you're distilling isn't really facts or even output distributions, it's a behavior: the habit of thinking longer, backtracking, checking work. And that turned out to transfer surprisingly well through plain SFT on reasoning traces. A small model can pick up the pattern of long chain-of-thought from a few hundred thousand examples in a way that's pretty hard to get through RL from scratch at that scale. Which raises the question of whether what we're calling distillation is sometimes more like teaching a procedure than compressing a function.

So if I had to give a one-sentence answer: distillation today means using a stronger model as the training signal for a weaker one, and the interesting research questions are all about what form that signal takes, whose samples it's computed on, and what it's actually transferring.

r001.rationale: The response describes a larger teacher and smaller student, but never says they can be the same size.

r002.rationale: It describes alternatives to fine-tuning on teacher-generated samples, including matching teacher logits on student-generated trajectories and using a reward signal.

astra-6.text:
I think distillation has become a broader term than it used to be. Traditionally, you had a large teacher model and a smaller student model, and you trained the student to match the teacher’s output distribution. The idea was to retain as much of the teacher’s capability as possible while making inference cheaper.

Today, people also use distillation to describe training on outputs generated by another model. The teacher might produce answers, explanations, or reasoning traces, and those become training data for the student. You don’t necessarily need access to the teacher’s probabilities, and the student doesn’t even have to be smaller.

The common thread is transferring behavior from one model to another. But the details matter: what does the teacher generate, on which inputs, and how does the student learn from it? Matching probabilities and fine-tuning on generated reasoning are both called distillation, but they provide quite different learning signals.

r001.rationale: It says the student “doesn’t even have to be smaller,” which includes a student the same size as the teacher.

r002.rationale: It describes traditional distillation as matching the teacher’s output distribution, alongside training on teacher-generated data, so distillation is not limited to the latter.

sol-6.1.text:
I think distillation has become a fairly broad term. Traditionally, you have a larger teacher model and a smaller student, and you train the student to match the teacher’s output distribution. The idea is to transfer much of the teacher’s capability into a model that’s cheaper to run.

Today, people also use it to mean training on outputs generated by another model. That could be answers, reasoning traces, or synthetic instruction data. You don’t necessarily need access to the teacher’s probabilities, and the student doesn’t necessarily have to be smaller.

So when someone says “distillation,” I think the useful follow-up is: what exactly are you transferring? Are you matching predictions, learning from demonstrations, or trying to reproduce a reasoning process? Those are related, but they give the student different kinds of supervision.

r001.rationale: It says the student “doesn’t necessarily have to be smaller,” which allows a student the same size as its teacher.

r002.rationale: It describes traditional distillation as matching the teacher’s output distribution, alongside training on teacher-generated outputs, so distillation is not limited to the latter.
